379.s: Most Latin arrangers ignore the bass foundation, which makes his band sound different.

379.t: Insisting on the rhythm section with Gillespie
379.s: He refuses to let Machito's recording sound like American jazz and instructs the bassist.
379.q: Even in the last -- the last (inaudible) with Gillespie, they got mad. I know they got mad. He and Dizzy, I say, Dizzy, I don't want this to sound like American (inaudible) playing big jazz. 243.t: Positions on the bass and taking bass solos
243.s: He says New Orleans players mostly stay in the first to third positions, and that he is not a bass soloist.
243.q: Oh well that all depends on the bass player itself. I mean the majority of New Orleans bass players, I mean they tend to play in first to third position most of the time. But sometimes the number gets loose and you feel like showing off or you run around there because I mean I do it a lot of times…

635.t: Proving his two-beat bass to symphony bassists
635.s: A symphony bassist doubts Foster's rhythm, and Foster offers to prove it with a piano player; he says he took the rhythm from a pianist's left hand.

1011.t: Thirds in the bass and guitar-based writing today
1011.s: Conniff says many young writers write from guitar and miss the beauty of the third in the bass he learned from Tchaikovsky; Rowe cites Bernstein.
1011.q: No, no, no, no. Larry King. He had Eric Clapton on. And he was playing guitar, and I think except the way I heard him and his writings with the guitar, mainly today, well a point I want to make is a lot of today’s music is being written by guitar players. 131.s: He explains what he wants from bassists and why they should stand up.
131.q: So when I see a guy sitting down, his feet aren’t even on the floor, half the time they’re up on the thing, what are you playing with? It’s coming from your head to your fingers. It’s supposed to come right straight through your body. For me.

494.t: What he wants from a bassist
494.s: A good sound, good time, and staying in the bottom register.
494.q: No, seriously, that’s – somebody’s going to make me sound good. What does that take? I like bass players who play – nice sound, good time. I don’t like bass players who play in the upper register a lot, because it makes what I play sound thin. So that’s not a requirement, but I like for bass…

135.t: Heath's concept of building a walking bass line
135.s: Heath explains Walter Page, strong and weak beats, and implying harmony while staying the foundation, plus John Lewis's role as teacher.
135.ch: Founding the MJQ and bass craft
135.q: Walter Page had played a bass line, and I took that bass line, which is basic blues bass line, and I put some notes in between notes, which is a concept that I have. If I was a bass teacher to teach young people to play the bass--jazz, there’s certain beats in jazz that are strong and the weaker…

506.t: Carrying the weight of the bass chair
506.s: Carter says the bass's role is directing the band and criticizes younger bassists for guitaristic habits.
506.q: And if the guy who has a bass in his hand is aware of that and has some talent, has some harmonic daring, he has some other rhythmic interests, he's listening to where he is in this puzzle of these strange players to him, he's willing to sacrifice what he does, his thing, to make this music work.…

428.t: Bassists who play high in the register

13.t: His first bass solo on Tantalizing a Cuban
13.s: Soloing was hard; small combos later forced him to solo.
